items.title: Exact chiral symmetry, non-Hermiticity, and the axial anomaly on the lattice: A symmetry-class criterion for disorder-induced undoubling
items.summary: A lattice Dirac operator designed to preserve exact chiral symmetry by weighting the derivative with a quenched random field---the \emph{chiral disordered fermions} (\CDF) of [L.\ Jacobs, Phys.\ Rev.\ Lett.\ \textbf{51}, 172 (1983)]---is reexamined with modern tools. We show that the disorder-averaged operator satisfies $\anticomm{\Deff}{\gfive}=0$ exactly, to all orders in disorder strength. Disorder lifts the doubler degeneracy, driving doublers off the real axis into a complex mass while the physical mode remains protected, but does so through non-Hermiticity rather than a Ginsparg--Wilson relation. Consequently the axial index vanishes in every formulation: the Hermitian trace $\Tr(\gfive D)$, the bi-orthogonal index for non-Hermitian operators, and the algebraic Riesz-projector index, including at exceptional points. The \CDF operator therefore cannot reproduce the axial anomaly: its failure is enforced by the exact chiral symmetry it preserves. We classify neighboring constructions by the Dirac channel carrying the lattice structure. Disorder in the $\g_\mu$ channel preserves chirality, realizes an Altland--Zirnbauer chiral class, and cannot carry an index; disorder in the $\mathbb{1}$ mass channel breaks chiral symmetry and yields Callan--Harvey/domain-wall physics. A one-parameter family interpolates between them, with the 1983 operator and Kaplan's domain wall as opposite limits, distinguished not by disorder itself but by the channel it occupies. This unifies lattice-QCD undoubling with the tenfold-way classification of disordered Dirac fermions and settles the disorder route to chiral lattice fermions.

items.title: How much data does a memory kernel need? Measurement requirements for fractional models of battery and corrosion degradation
items.summary: How much data does a memory kernel need before a fit is meaningful? For a distributed-order model, the answer is about 3.1 decades of observation, more than standard battery-degradation tests provide. Battery capacity fade and corrosion-film growth depend on their history, so they are often modelled using general fractional calculus (GFC), where memory is described by an arbitrary Sonine kernel rather than a single power law. We tested this using two mechanistic models without fractional operators and de Levie's porous-electrode model, whose high-frequency order is exactly 0.5; our estimator recovered 0.500. A single aging curve can recover an effective order, alpha, to within 5% noise using a weak formulation, while separating the tempered parameters (alpha, lambda) requires several Arrhenius conditions, with errors improving from (0.25, 0.43) with one condition to (0.04, 0.07) with four. A distributed-order memory needs 3.1 decades of data to be resolved to 90%; below that, a two-order memory can collapse into one intermediate order that fits the data better than the true spectrum. For saturating passivation, however, a general kernel improves the fit substantially, raising R2 from 0.862 to 0.998. Across 20 cells from two public datasets, observation windows span only 1.23 to 2.24 decades, making the 3.1-decade result a practical design rule: it defines what must be measured before fitting a memory kernel, not only what cannot be fitted.

items.title: Molecular and Nanoscale Control of Exciton Transfer in TADF-Sensitized Fluorescence
authors: Tunan Kuang, Chunhui Zhang, Ran Fang, Mengna Yu, Quanyou Feng, and Linghai Xie
items.summary: Abstract TADF-sensitized fluorescence (TSF), also known as hyperfluorescence, combines efficient triplet exciton harvesting with the narrowband emission of fluorescent emitters. Yet, its performance depends on the interplay between exciton conversion, energy transfer, and molecular organization across different length scales. Herein, we review recent progress in nanoscale exciton-transfer engineering for TSF, with emphasis on molecular excited-state dynamics, sensitizer-dopant spatial control, diversified energy-transfer pathways, and interlayer sensitization. These approaches regulate exciton conversion and lifetime, balance Förster and Dexter energy transfer, and control exciton distribution within emissive layers and across interfaces. We also discuss emerging directions including kinetic matching, spatial organization, and multiscale modeling for understanding the links between molecular structure, energy-transfer dynamics, and device performance. This Mini-Review provides profound insights into transforming random blend systems into controllable nanoscale exciton-transfer networks, paving the way for efficient narrowband TSF OLEDs.

items.title: Light-Induced Néel Vector Reversal in 2D van der Waals Antiferromagnets
authors: Yangyang Feng, Ying Dai, Baibiao Huang, and Yandong Ma
items.summary: Abstract Antiferromagnetic spintronics promises ultrafast device performance, yet the essential Néel vector reversal is hindered by its intrinsic immunity to external magnetic fields. Here, we propose a mechanism for deterministic Néel vector reversal in 2D van der Waals antiferromagnets enabled by ultrafast laser pulses. The core physics involves light-induced asymmetric interlayer demagnetization, which drives the antiferromagnet into a transient ferrimagnetic state with a finite net moment. This transient symmetry breaking allows the Néel vector to be controlled by an external magnetic field. We identify that the intrinsic structural and electronic asymmetries and spin–orbit-coupling mediated spin flips are essential for this process. Using first-principles calculations and real-time time-dependent density functional theory, we further demonstrate this mechanism in bilayer NiICl and YI 2 . Our work establishes a general strategy for the optical manipulation of 2D antiferromagnetic order.

items.title: Count the climate losses we prevent
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79128-x Climate adaptation reduces losses, but successful risk reduction often leaves no claim or expenditure that records the benefit. Avoided-loss accounts would preserve intervention-specific estimates and evidence across insurance, lending and public finance, without recognizing counterfactual losses as assets.

items.title: Diacylglycerol Metabolism Drives Host–pathogen Responses During Enteric Infection in Drosophila
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79306-x Li et al. reveal a lipid-dependent signaling axis that links intestinal epithelial cells and intestinal muscle to gut motility and bacterial pathogen clearance, offering mechanistic insight into how lipid dynamics orchestrate host defenses.

items.title: Molecular-level control of nitrogen sites enables CO 2 electro-reduction under industrially relevant conditions
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79247-5 Direct conversion of dilute carbon dioxide requires catalysts that maintain access to scarce reactants. Here, the authors show that enriching pyridinic nitrogen near nickel active sites promotes local carbon dioxide capture and selective conversion to carbon monoxide.

items.title: Recent extreme heatwaves are no match for future events
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-76809-5 This paper shows that current temperature and emission-reduction targets provide only limited protection against future heatwaves, which are found to surpass recent exceptional events across multiple regions of the world.

items.title: Toward Ternary Computing Enabled by Origami-Inspired Modular Architectures
items.summary: Nature Communications, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79187-0 The work presents an origami-based modular mechanical computing architecture that uses multi-stable states and programmed kinematic responses to define a generalized paradigm scalable to multi-valued computing, demonstrated in binary and ternary logic and arithmetic, overcoming gate-cascading limits.

items.title: Oxygen-Stoichiometry-Driven Crossover from Polaronic Insulator to Superconductor in Orthorhombic Ti9O10 Films
authors: Zongyao Huang, 宗耀 黄, Wei Hu, 卫 胡, Zhiwei Wang, 智炜 王, Shihao Liu, 仕豪 刘, Huiyu Wang, 慧宇 王, Yanjun Li, 彦君 李, Xiangyu Hua, 翔宇 华, Zhaohang Li, 朝航 李, Feixiong Quan, 飞熊 全, Zhengjie Wang, 郑杰 王, Ying Feng, 颖 冯, Zhen Wang, 臻 王, Jing Tao, 婧 陶, Xigang Luo, 习刚 罗, Jianjun Ying, 剑俊 应, Tao Wu, 涛 吴, Xianhui Chen and 仙辉 陈
items.summary: The Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer theory of superconductivity is restricted to weak electron–phonon coupling. In the strong-coupling regime, charge carriers self-trap via local lattice distortions, forming polarons whose condensation provides an alternative mechanism for superconductivity. Titanium oxides serve as a model system for polaron physics, suggesting the possibility of polaronic superconductivity. Here we report oxygen-stoichiometry-driven crossover from polaronic insulator to superconductor in epitaxial Ti9O10 thin films. Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy supports the films as a potential polaronic insulator, in which oxygen stoichiometry control reveals an anticorrelation between the polaronic insulating state and superconductivity. Tuning the oxygen pressure suppresses the polaronic insulating state and induces superconductivity, resulting in two distinct superconducting regions in the oxygen–pressure phase diagram. Our results provide a pathway toward understanding superconductivity in polaronic materials and offer a route for searching high-temperature superconductors.

items.title: Medium Electrical Conductivity Governs the Collective Behaviors of Quincke Rollers
authors: Zihan Qiao, 子涵 乔, Jingrui Gu, 京瑞 顾, Jiayu Liu, 佳钰 刘, Guomeng Wang, 国猛 王, Hao Lu, 灏 卢, Ting Kuang, 婷 况, Bo Zhang, 波 张, Wei Wang and 威 王
items.summary: Active matter systems can convert environmental energy into continuous motion and exhibit collective behaviors. As a typical electrically driven active particle system, Quincke rollers can display a variety of collective behaviors under a uniform DC electric field. However, a systematic understanding of the emergence and evolution of different collective behaviors is still lacking, and it remains unclear how external environmental conditions, such as temperature and humidity, influence the dynamics of collective behaviors. In this work, we find that increasing temperature and humidity drives a continuous transition of the collective behavior of Quincke rollers from vortices to polar clusters, rotating clusters, and finally active crystals. In situ electrical measurements show that the medium conductivity increases by nearly 10-fold as the temperature rises from 20 ℃ to 60 ℃, and by approximately 30-fold as the relative humidity increases from 5% to 65%, whereas the permittivity changes by about 10−15%. Finite-element calculations further reveal that the increase in medium electrical conductivity strongly modifies the magnitudes of the electric dipolar and hydrodynamic interactions between rollers. These forces shift from pure repulsion to anisotropic attraction and then to isotropic attraction, resulting in the emergence of vortices, polar clusters, rotating clusters, and active crystals in turn. These results provide a simple physical picture linking the conductivity of the medium to the collective states in Quincke roller system and establish a theoretical framework that incorporates dipolar interaction, hydrodynamic interaction, and electro-hydrodynamic interaction for understanding the dynamics of collective behavior. In addition, this work demonstrates that temperature and humidity can serve as simple, efficient, and reversible control parameters for the in situ regulation of the collective behaviors of Quincke rollers.

items.title: Power-Law Quasiperiodic Criticality in a Non-Hermitian Ising Chain
authors: Wen-Long You and 文龙 尤
items.summary: We study a non-Hermitian Ising chain with a power-law quasiperiodic field hj = hcosp(2παj+ϕ), where the positive integer p controls the power of the modulation. The model admits an exact site-factorized similarity transformation that maps the quasi-Hermitian regime onto a real quasiperiodic Ising chain. We derive the exact zero-mode edge-localization boundary and show that the critical field on the quasi-Hermitian branch scales as 2p, while the associated localization-length exponent remains unity for all p. At the boundary, the variance of the logarithmic coupling fluctuations is enhanced exactly by a factor of p2. In the quasi-Hermitian regime, the factorized similarity transformation shows that the spatial biorthogonal entanglement spectrum is identical to that of the Hermitian counterpart. The half-chain entanglement entropy exhibits approximately logarithmic growth over the accessible sizes, with a p-dependent finite-size slope. We finally discuss a possible realization using state-selective loss and conditional no-jump dynamics.

items.title: Giant Planar Hall Effect of Unprecedented Amplitude in n-HgTe with Extremely Low Electron Density
authors: A.T. Lonchakov, S.B. Bobin and S.D. Popov
items.summary: We report the observation of a giant planar Hall effect in an n-HgTe single crystal with an extremely low electron density of 7.3×1014 cm−3. Its amplitude reaches an unprecedented value of 0.9 Ohm·cm at T = 40 K and in a magnetic field of 10 T—to the best of our knowledge, the highest ever reported for this effect in any topological material. We attribute the strong magnetoresistance anisotropy underlying the giant planar Hall effect to the coexistence of a topological Weyl semimetal phase and a trivial gapless phase in the band spectrum of a bulk n-HgTe. The former gives rise to strong negative longitudinal magnetoresistance driven by chiral anomaly, whereas the latter leads to charge compensation-induced positive transverse magnetoresistance without saturation. We have established that it is precisely this magnetoresistance that provides the dominant contribution to the giant amplitude of the planar Hall effect. The observed giant planar Hall effect in this particular n-HgTe sample suggests that low-density mercury telluride merits further investigation as a candidate material for exploring chiral-anomaly transport and for potential sensor applications.

items.title: Electron–Phonon Coupling Drives the Gapless Charge Density Wave in Few-Layer 1T-VSe2
authors: Yonglong Cheng, 咏龙 程, Yimanqi He, 逸蔓奇 何, Xiangfan Xu and 象繁 徐
items.summary: The driving mechanism of the charge density wave (CDW) remains debated, particularly between Fermi surface nesting (FSN) and electron–phonon coupling (EPC) scenarios. Here, gate-tunable electrical and thermoelectric transport measurements were used to probe the CDW-related electronic structure in few-layer 1T-VSe2. Thickness reduction strongly suppresses the long-range three-dimensional CDW order associated with the bulk transition near 110 K, allowing the high-temperature CDW-related anomaly near 170 K to be resolved in macroscopic transport. Through gate tuning, we find that this CDW-related state does not exhibit signatures of a well-defined Peierls-like gap but instead remains gapless within an intrinsic multiband electronic landscape. In particular, the Seebeck coefficient shows pronounced anomalies at both temperature scales (110 K and 170 K), yet no gap-induced thermoelectric anomaly or gate-dependent gap-opening behavior is observed. These results demonstrate the gapless nature of the CDW state, while the high-temperature 170 K anomaly directly fingerprints the localized precursor lattice softening, collectively providing strong transport evidence that supports EPC over conventional FSN as the dominant driving mechanism. Our work provides a new experimental perspective on the dimensionality-dependent CDW behavior in VSe2 and establishes thermoelectric transport as a sensitive probe for distinguishing CDW formation mechanisms in low-dimensional materials.

items.title: In-Plane Heterostructures Enable Deterministic and Repeated Biomolecular Sensing by Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering
authors: Lijun Meng, Shitong Zhang, Min Qiu, Zhigang Wang, Jinyi Tong, and Ruhong Zhou
items.summary: Abstract Applications of plasmonic nanopores for molecular sequencing remain limited by poorly controlled translocation dynamics and predominantly single-pass readout. Here, we propose an in-plane heterostructure architecture that integrates molecular transport, confinement, and surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) readout to enable deterministic and repeated interrogation of individual biomolecules. Using all-atom molecular dynamics coupled with nanoplasmonic simulations, we show that the heterostructure can actively guide molecules into and through a localized sensing region while constraining their conformational and translational dynamics. Simulated SERS signatures discriminate single-stranded DNA sequences with resolution approaching the single-nucleobase scale and further suggest the feasibility of distinguishing polyglutamine tracts of different lengths. Importantly, the in-plane geometry allows molecules to be controllably transported back and forth across the sensing region, providing a route to repeated measurements of the same molecule rather than relying on stochastic single-pass translocation. These results suggest a strategy for improving the accuracy and reproducibility of nanopore-based biomolecular sensing.

items.title: Large-Tiny Spin-Stripe SDW Order in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ via $^{139}$La-NQR Spectroscopy: Reconsideration Based on the $Am2m$ Structure
items.summary: The lower-symmetry $Am2m$ structure was recently proposed as the intrinsic ambient-pressure phase of La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ based on synchrotron x-ray diffraction, whereas earlier studies investigated its properties assuming the commonly accepted $Amam$ structure. Here, we reexamine the crystal structure in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ and the spin configuration of spin-density-wave (SDW) state via $^{139}$La nuclear quadrupole resonance (NQR). The observation of two distinct La(2) sites in the NQR spectra is naturally accounted for by the $Am2m$ structure without any special assumptions, whereas it cannot be reconciled within the $Amam$ framework. Within the $Am2m$ framework, we reanalyze the spin configuration of the SDW phase and identify it as a large-tiny spin-stripe structure, arising naturally from two inequivalent Ni sites with large and tiny magnetic moments. These results establish the itinerant nature of the SDW order at ambient pressure in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, providing a basis for understanding its relationship to the emergence of high-$T_c$ superconductivity under high pressure.

items.title: Emergent thermal fluctuations and non-Hermitian phase transitions in open photon condensates
items.summary: Driven-dissipative Bose-Einstein condensates of photons in optical resonators have been shown theoretically to exist as a long-lived, yet metastable state stabilized by a ghost attractor, despite continuous driving [Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 053402 (2025)]. Here we analyze the properties of this metastable condensate as well as the relaxation dynamics into and out of this state by means of the Lindblad master-equation approach, treating the condensate and the equal-time, noncondensed fluctuations on the same footing. Despite its nonequilibrium origin, the quasistationary condensate exhibits thermal behavior in that the order-parameter fluctuations scale with system size as in thermodynamic equilibrium, and the photon-number distribution in multimode resonators is in excellent agreement with a Bose-Einstein distribution. A linear stability analysis further reveals the presence of several exceptional points, resulting in multiple non-Hermitian phase transitions associated with the relaxation dynamics into and out of the metastable condensate. These behaviors reconcile apparently contradictory experimental results.

items.title: Charged Three-Dimensional Solitons in a Ferroelectric Nematic Liquid Crystal
items.summary: Experimental observations and computer simulation of formation and structural properties of so far experimentally never seen electrically charged propagating 3D solitons are reported. The propagating solitons appear spontaneously without an external field in a ferroelectric nematic (NF) liquid crystal under rapid cooling from the antiferroelectric (SmZA) phase. The observed solitons propagate either parallel or antiparallel to the ferroelectric polarization and annihilate when they collide with each other. They are attributed to either positively or negatively charged propagating local polarization splay formed to screen excess negative or positive mobile charge lumps in the NF phase. The presence of mobile charge is attributed to a spatially periodic charge distribution present in the antiferroelectric phase that temporarily remains after the temperature is quenched through the antiferroelectric- ferroelectric phase transition.

items.title: Tree tensor network states represent low-energy states faithfully
items.summary: Extending corresponding results for matrix product states [Verstraete and Cirac, PRB 73, 094423 (2006); Schuch et al. PRL 100, 030504 (2008)], it is shown how the approximation error of tree tensor network states (TTNS) can be bounded using Schmidt spectra or Rényi entanglement entropies of the target quantum state. Conversely, one obtains bounds on TTNS bond dimensions needed to achieve a specific approximation accuracy. The result implies that efficient TTNS approximations exist if $α<1$ Rényi entanglement entropies for single-branch cuts obey an area law, as in ground and low-energy states of certain gapped systems on tree graphs.

items.title: Odd Capillarity
items.summary: Capillarity governs interfacial relaxation and hydrodynamic motion in binary fluids through parity-even mechanical stresses. Here, we introduce \emph{odd capillarity}, a parity-breaking interfacial mechanical response, by incorporating a symmetric, nonvariational, parity-odd capillary stress into the Cahn--Hilliard--Navier--Stokes (CHNS) equations. This stress generates forces along interfaces, transverse to ordinary capillary forces, and performs mechanical work that is not balanced by changes in the composition free energy. Direct numerical simulations reveal that odd capillarity arrests domain coarsening while sustaining turbulent fluid motion without a conventional inertial energy cascade, as energy injection is predominantly balanced by viscous dissipation. In asymmetric mixtures, odd capillarity driven deformation and breakup interrupt droplet growth, producing dynamically arrested emulsions with composition hyperuniformity and suppressed large-scale vorticity fluctuations. These findings establish odd capillarity as a distinct interfacial mechanism for controlling phase separation and sustaining nonequilibrium fluid motion.

items.title: Simulating a chiral gauge theory
items.summary: Chiral gauge theories underlie the Standard Model, yet none has been simulated nonperturbatively. Lattice constructions that evade the Nielsen-Ninomiya obstruction entail complex fermion measures or infinite-dimensional local Hilbert spaces. Here we provide a gauge-invariant Hamiltonian lattice regularization of 1+1-dimensional abelian chiral gauge theories built from clock-and-shift qudits with $\mathbb{Z}_N$ gauge fields, in which the global chiral symmetry and its 't Hooft anomaly survive exactly mod $N$. Anomaly cancellation on the lattice lets the Gauss laws be imposed and solved exactly, reducing the theory to an unconstrained qudit chain. Using infinite matrix product states, we simulate the canonical 1+1-dimensional chiral gauge theory, the 34-50 model, and find excellent agreement with analytic predictions, showing that a finite-dimensional local Hilbert space at $N=6$ reproduces the expected infrared physics of the continuum 34-50 model. This provides an efficient and practical solution to the problem of simulating general abelian chiral gauge theories in 1+1 dimensions, both on classical and quantum computers.

items.title: Density Modulations of Zero Sound
items.summary: We study the density modulation of an interacting Fermi gas caused by the uniform motion of an impurity at zero temperature. For strong enough interaction among Fermi atoms, the modulation propagates thanks to the excitation of the collective zero sound mode if the impurity speed is above the zero sound threshold. We are able to assess, via a semi-analytic evaluation, the extent of the zero sound contribution to the density oscillation over and above the incoherent background of particle-hole excitations. Given the strong dependence of the results on the features of the gas interaction potential, we also analyze how they vary depending on its strength, range and shape.

items.title: Longitudinal and Transverse Thermoelectric Properties in Topological Quantum Materials
items.summary: Thermoelectric materials can be topologically trivial or non-trivial, enabling reversible interconversion of heat and electricity using a solid-state technology. Incidentally, few of the first experimentally discovered 3D topological materials, namely, Bi, Sb, Sn and Pb-based chalcogenides, were long known as good thermoelectric materials. In these compounds, the heavy atoms that give rise to strong spin-orbit coupling often become essential for band inversion and non-trivial band topology. They lead to low lattice thermal conductivity, linearly dispersing Dirac-like bands induce high electrical mobility, and a band-inverted electronic structure with multiple band extrema gives rise to high Seebeck coefficients. In materials, where the applied temperature gradient induces electrical voltage (Seebeck effect) in the same direction, they are termed as longitudinal thermoelectrics. On the other hand, when the generated electrical voltage and applied thermal current remain orthogonal to each other, the materials are termed as transverse thermoelectrics. The transverse response can be driven by an additional external magnetic field (ordinary Nernst effect), intrinsic remanent magnetisation, or non-zero Berry curvature of a material, which arises from their non-trivial topology (anomalous Nernst effect). We discuss another class of quantum materials, known as goniopolar materials, that exhibit axis-dependent conduction polarity and hence transverse thermoelectric effects, which are based on mechanisms of longitudinal thermoelectric properties. In this review, we cover both types of thermoelectricity, focusing on materials that possess non-trivial topological order. We make connections between their structures, topology and transport properties and suggest tunability of thermoelectric properties going beyond conventional mechanisms such as electron-phonon interactions.

items.title: Energy-filtered readout preserves gap-enhanced sensing in interacting quantum dots
items.summary: A small excitation gap makes a quantum dot a sensitive probe of a weak electric field, but the charge detector reading it can also excite it. We calculate how much of this enhancement survives continuous readout for two interacting electrons tuned through a confinement-driven crossover in a gate-defined dot. The probe is a few-level system read by a weakly coupled linear detector, with second-order transition rates and information from the mean detector current, for gaps up to a few hundred microelectronvolts, couplings up to 50 $μ$eV and temperatures up to 100 mK. The outcome depends on the energy structure of the detector, not only its noise. A quantum point contact measures more strongly at higher bias but, once the bias energy exceeds the gap, also excites the probe; when this back-action dominates the relaxation of the probe, the optimised information rate grows only as the inverse of the gap. A sensor quantum dot with a narrow level instead reaches full strength at a bias below the gap, where a non-interacting detector cannot excite it at zero temperature. This energy-filtered readout keeps the inverse-square gap dependence of the quantum Fisher information down to gaps comparable to the level width of the detector or ten times the thermal energy. At the tested operating points, higher probe states change the sensitivities by up to 6% and the exponents by up to 0.06; coherence corrections to the populations and transduced signal are negligible, and any gain from the full detector record is unresolved within 1-2% numerical uncertainty. Under the same conditions the interacting pair gives about three times the information rate of a single electron with the same gap and detector, for contact and Coulomb-type interactions alike. The different gap dependences and optimal biases of the two detectors can be tested by bias and gate sweeps on charge-sensed double dots.

items.title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials
items.summary: Grain growth during heat treatment strongly affects the microstructure of polycrystalline materials and, consequently, their mechanical properties. Although numerical methods such as front-tracking or front-capturing simulations can accurately describe grain growth, their high computational cost limits their use for long or non-isothermal thermal cycles. In previous work, grain growth was successfully predicted under isothermal conditions by treating grain size distributions as time series and forecasting their evolution using recurrent neural networks, allowing complete grain growth trajectories to be generated in seconds rather than through costly PDE-based simulations. In the present work, this forecasting framework is reformulated to handle non-isothermal conditions by explicitly incorporating thermal information into the model architecture. Grain size distributions are encoded using a convolutional neural network, thermal descriptors are embedded through a dedicated multilayer perceptron, and temporal evolution is predicted using a recurrent network. Instantaneous temperature and thermal rate are provided at each time step, allowing the model to adapt its predictions to changing thermal conditions. The framework is trained and evaluated on datasets generated from validated front-tracking simulations across a wide range of non-isothermal thermal paths. The results show that the thermally conditioned model accurately reproduces grain growth dynamics under complex thermal histories, achieving, in k-fold cross-validation over all simulations, mean relative errors of 2.99% (one-hour cycles) and 4.51% (four-hour cycles) with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.99, and mean relative errors between 1.91% and 14.66% on ten simulations following four unseen thermal histories of increasing complexity.

items.title: A direct algebraic proof for the non-positivity of Liouvillian spectral values and controlling the dissipative gap of unital systems
items.summary: Markovian open quantum systems are described by the Lindblad master equation $\partial_tρ=\mathcal{L}(ρ)$, where $ρ$ denotes the system's density operator and $\mathcal{L}$ the Liouville super-operator, which is also known as the Liouvillian. For systems with a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, it is a fundamental property of the Liouvillian that the real parts of all its eigenvalues are non-positive. Analogously, for infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, the Liouvillian as a map on trace-class operators only has spectral values with non-positive real parts. The usual arguments for these properties are indirect, using that $\mathcal{L}$ generates a quantum channel and that quantum channels are contractive. We provide a direct algebraic proof based on the Lindblad form of Liouvillians. Subtleties for infinite-dimensional systems are highlighted. For example, unbounded operators can then be eigenvectors of the adjoint Liouvillian with positive eigenvalues, corresponding to a physical instability of the system. As an illustrative application of the algebraic approach, we prove that a strict minimum can be imposed on the dissipative gap of any unital Markovian spin-$s$ or fermionic many-particle system by adding simple local dissipators. The added dissipators comprise Pauli or generalized Pauli Lindblad operators for spin systems and Majorana Lindblad operators for fermionic systems.

items.title: Experimental evaluation of Kolmogorov's first similarity hypothesis for shear-dependent viscosity fluids
items.summary: We experimentally investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov's first similarity hypothesis to shear-dependent viscosity fluids. We assess whether dissipative range statistics exhibit a self-similar behavior in nearly homogeneous and isotropic turbulence, using stereo particle image velocimetry in aqueous Carbopol solutions across two concentrations and a range of forcing conditions. We observe that, when normalized by the mean viscosity and mean dissipation rate, second- and third-order structure functions collapse across the different experimental conditions and exhibit functional forms compatible with classical Newtonian results. These observations are in general agreement with the recent numerical results of Rosti [J. Fluid Mech. 1012, R5 (2025)], who proposed that Kolmogorov's similarity hypotheses can be extended to shear-thinning fluids by considering dissipation scales based on the mean viscosity, the mean dissipation rate, and the flow index.

items.title: Quantum Spin Wave Theory with Multi-Spin Interactions for Magnetic Materials Modeling
items.summary: In the field of magnetism within condensed matter physics, magnetic systems are microscopically described by a spin Hamiltonian. Its parameterization is accessible through both ab initio calculations and fits to experimental data. Frequently, this is achieved via multi-stage calculations that either relate the parameters to observable material properties or map a Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian onto an effective spin model. In this realm, accurate and flexible methods are essential for simulating the physical properties of the latter. The present study focuses on one such method: spin wave theory. The approach is applied to a new formulation of the spin Hamiltonian, named polynomial localized spin model (PLSM), which includes terms of arbitrary order in the spin operators. This enables the direct application of linear spin wave theory (LSWT) to the analysis of the energy landscape and spin-wave spectrum of arbitrary collinear and non-collinear phases in any realistic magnetic material. Moreover, the classical and quantum parts of the PLSM are cleanly separated. Finally, an open-source implementation of LSWT, named Magnopy, is presented. It interfaces with modern parameterization software, supports arbitrary collinear and non-collinear systems, and is designed for both scripting and standalone use.

items.title: Strain-Glass Dynamics in the Superionic Conductor Na$_3$PS$_4$
items.summary: Ionic conduction in solid-state electrolytes is conventionally described by mobile cations migrating through a static host lattice. Yet the fastest conductors are often the most disordered, and how disorder enhances transport remains unresolved at the mesoscale, inaccessible to ensemble-averaged probes. We use Bragg X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy to measure nanoscale structural dynamics of a single ball-milled Na$_3$PS$_4$ particle. We find that the cubic phase behaves as a strain glass: a frustrated configuration of three degenerate tetragonal variants with short-range order. Its domain-wall motion is stress-driven, crossing over irreversibly to thermally activated dynamics on annealing as residual milling stress is depleted. Rearrangements follow scale-free avalanche statistics, matching ferroelastic martensites but without external driving. The tetragonal polymorph shows none of these features and relaxes fifty times more slowly. These dynamics occur on timescales comparable to estimated ionic diffusion across the particle, indicating the host structure cannot be assumed static on transport-relevant timescales.

items.title: High temperature Jahn-Teller distortion and short-range order in CsCuCl$_3$
items.summary: CsCuCl$_3$, chiral and Jahn-Teller distorted at room temperature, takes a more symmetric structure above 423 K. Describing this 'simpler' high temperature structure is far from simple and has been the subject of many, sometimes contradicting, studies. Here we reinvestigate the high temperature structure of CsCuCl$_3$, its thermal stability, and its effect on room temperature chirality. In situ pair distribution function data from powder neutron diffraction confirms that CsCuCl$_3$ is Jahn-Teller distorted both below and above $T_\mathrm{c}$, and provides a quantitative view of short-range order in the high temperature structure. In situ powder x-ray diffraction shows that CsCuCl$_3$ does not undergo any additional structural changes above 423 K and is congruently melting. In situ single crystal x-ray diffraction experiments reveal that the phase transition induces domains of mixed handedness in originally homochiral crystals. These findings contribute to a better understanding of phase transitions in Jahn-Teller distorted compounds, and highlight the potential use of phase transitions to control chiral domains.

items.title: Scalable Generative Sampling and Multilevel Estimation for Lattice Field Theories Near Criticality
items.summary: Sampling lattice field theories near criticality is severely hindered by critical slowing down, which makes standard Markov chain methods increasingly inefficient at large lattice volumes. We introduce a multiscale generative sampler, inspired by renormalization-group ideas, that models the Boltzmann distribution through a coarse-to-fine hierarchy across length scales. At each level, a conditional Gaussian mixture model captures the main local dependence of newly introduced variables on the already-sampled coarse field, while a masked continuous normalizing flow refines the remaining conditional structure. Coarse levels encode the dominant long-wavelength modes, and finer levels progressively add short-distance fluctuations. In addition, because the architecture preserves coarse fields exactly during refinement, it provides exact restriction maps at no additional computational cost and directly enables asymptotically unbiased Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) variance reduction. For the two-dimensional scalar $φ^4$ theory near criticality, the method achieves integrated autocorrelation times orders of magnitude smaller than Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) on large volumes, maintains high importance-sampling efficiency relative to other generative baselines, and reproduces asymptotically unbiased physical observables in statistical agreement with long HMC simulations.

items.title: Hall-Density Collapse as Direct Evidence for Percolative Conduction Onset in Monolayer MoS$_2$ Transistors
authors: C. J. L. de la Rosa
items.summary: The origin of the apparent metal-insulator transition in two-dimensional electron systems remains debated. Using temperature-dependent transport and Hall measurements on industry-relevant MoS$_2$ monolayer FETs with amorphous HfO$_2$ dielectrics, we establish classical percolation as the underlying mechanism. We report two complementary signatures of disorder-driven conduction onset: a temperature-independent Hall-density collapse as a function of absolute gate voltage and a vanishing activation energy at a characteristic carrier density $n_{\mathrm{c}}$, identified as the percolation threshold. These findings identify dielectric-interface disorder, rather than channel quality alone, as the key parameter governing device turn-on. The extracted activation barriers reach values substantially exceeding room-temperature thermal energies, indicating that disorder-driven conduction onset remains relevant well beyond cryogenic transport.

items.title: Evolutionary Design of Interpretable Spatial Descriptors for Structure-Property Relationship Discovery
items.summary: Structure property prediction is a classical task in machine learning, ranging from molecular activity and materials properties to local functional responses measured in microscopy. For image-based regression, two choices define the information available to the predictor: the size of the image neighborhood and the spatial resolution retained within it. A small neighborhood can omit relevant surrounding structure, whereas a large, finely sampled neighborhood can introduce redundant or irrelevant information. Here, we develop a framework for constructing spatial descriptors for prediction of local spectra and hysteresis loops. We benchmark regression models, use SHAP maps to examine their spatial attribution, and explore the effect of the patch size and compression to establish the relationship between predictive accuracy and descriptor dimensionality. We then use a genetic algorithm to optimize spatial partitions and the assignment of mean, minimum, and maximum pooling operations. Each retained region contributes an explicit measurement of the image, allowing the search to balance prediction error against the number of descriptor values. Cartesian and polar constructions provide complementary ways to organize this information. The resulting descriptors make it possible to examine where spatial detail is needed, where regional summaries are sufficient, and how these choices depend on the predictor and the measured response. The same approach can be used for molecules and solids once the genetic algorithm rules for these are established.

items.title: Quantum Tunneling-induced Hybridization and Coherent Dynamics of Jackiw-Rebbi Zero Modes in a Modified Su-Schrieffer-Heeger Chain
items.summary: We investigate analytically and numerically the tunneling-induced hybridization and coherent dynamics of Jackiw-Rebbi zero modes in a modified Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model. Unlike the conventional SSH model, this modified system possess two bulk gap-closing points, namely the quadratic-type gap-closing point at momenta $k_0=0$ and the Dirac-type gap-closing points at $k_0=\pmπ/4a$. Although the quadratic point does not support a topological domain wall due to the absence of mass inversion, the low-energy Dirac theory around $k_0=\pmπ/4a$ predicts an effective mass that changes sign at two spatially separated domain walls under a kink profile, generating a pair of JR bound states with each states localized at one of those domain walls. We show that the finite spatial overlap between the JR zero modes lifts the zero-energy degeneracy through quantum tunneling, producing symmetric-antisymmetric hybridized states. Using an effective two-level description, we demonstrate that hybridized JR modes undergo coherent tunneling oscillations between the two domain walls, accompanied by periodic transfer of sublattice polarization between the (A,C) and (B,D) sectors. Our results establish a unified framework connecting JR zero modes, quantum tunneling, and coherent dynamics in modified SSH systems, offering a promising platform for controllable topological quantum-state transfer in engineered lattice structures.

items.title: Hidden entropic order of emergent charges in a classical Ampère spin liquid
items.summary: Classical spin liquids are characterized by an extensive number of ground-state configurations. Coulomb spin liquids have, in this ground-state manifold, a divergence-free local constraint, which gives dipolar correlations and pinch points in the structure factor. Recently, models with a complementary ground-state constraint, defined by a zero-circulation constraint (Ampère's law), have been proposed. While classical Coulomb spin liquids forbid emergent charges, their Ampère counterparts leave the charges unconstrained. Here we study an Ising Ampère model on the octochlore lattice. The ground states obey a Gauss law for an antisymmetric rank-two field, i.e., three coupled two-dimensional Gauss laws, which are expected to produce pinch points in the structure factor. Nevertheless, maximal charges, vertices with all six arrows in or out, spontaneously accumulate on one of the two sublattices of the cubic lattice, with disordered signs. This order has a purely entropic origin; it washes out the pinch-point singularities at large scales, produces no magnetic Bragg peaks, and coexists with an extensive entropy. The system enters into this sublattice long-range ordered state through a continuous transition in what seems to be the three-dimensional Ising universality class. Moreover, the state has no magnetic order; it is even under time reversal: it is a hidden, entropic order within the Ampère manifold. Thus, a system whose Gauss law would predict an algebraic spin liquid becomes, through a non-magnetic ordering transition, a partially ordered short-range spin liquid. Our study is based on a combination of the constraint-vector theory, exact bounds and enumeration, and Monte Carlo, Wang-Landau, and parallel-tempering simulations.

items.title: Ring Sliding-Bond Scission Interplay Affects Toughening in Mechanically Interlocked Networks
authors: Xiangrui Zheng, Zhuozheng Yu, Guoquan Liu, Xuzhou Yan, and Yang Wang
items.summary: Abstract Mechanically interlocked networks (MINs) built from [2]rotaxane cross-linkers combine high extensibility with enhanced toughness, yet how the interplay between ring mobility and bond scission influences their mechanical responses remains unclear. Here, we employ coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the deformation mechanisms of MINs with varying bond strength, strain rate, and graft density, where a crossover is observed in the deformation mechanism as bond strength increases. Specifically, the weak cross-links lead to scission-dominated deformation with negligible ring sliding, whereas MINs with strong cross-links exhibit profound ring sliding and inhibited bond scission, contributing to the enhanced toughness. Moreover, bond scission and ring sliding exhibit a strain-rate response with the lowest rate favoring scission over sliding, while reducing graft density delays the onset of both processes. These findings provide molecular insights for optimizing MIN mechanics by balancing movable-junction dynamics and cross-link stability.

items.title: A local Yang-Baxter obstruction for the hard-square model
items.summary: Many exact solutions of two-dimensional lattice models rest on an analytic family of weights satisfying the Yang-Baxter equation. The hard-hexagon model was solved in this way, while the neighbouring hard-square model has no known closed form. We determine the height alphabets that encode hard squares without hidden heights, and there are exactly two connected ones, the occupation variables themselves and the four heights of Andrews, Baxter and Forrester. Hard hexagons is integrable on both, but no analytic Yang-Baxter family of face weights passes through hard squares at nonzero activity on either. The difference lies in the exclusion rule, which for hard squares turns a few Yang-Baxter equations into polynomial identities that force auxiliary weights to vanish. A closed form for hard squares is not excluded, but a solution by this route would have to leave these encodings or go beyond a single analytic family through the model. Encodings with hidden heights remain open.

items.title: Unified Theory of Spin and Orbital Inverse Faraday Effects in Rashba Metals
items.summary: The inverse Faraday effect (IFE) offers a promising route toward optical control of magnetic moments in quantum materials. Yet experiments on spin-orbit-coupled metals indicate that no single microscopic mechanism suffices, implicating orbital currents alongside spin polarization. We derive both responses in a disordered Rashba metal using quantum kinetics and diagrammatics with impurity-renormalized optical vertices, providing the first unified diagrammatic derivation of spin and orbital IFE. Treating impurity scattering consistently, our number-conserving kinetic formulation restores full phase-space derivatives and the optical magnetic field neglected in earlier treatments. We connect nonlinear orbital magnetization to absorptive linear optical conductivity, revealing that the magnetic Lorentz force supplies half the orbital response. Our unified treatment resolves both channels across the Rashba resonance: spin IFE changes sign as frequency increases, while the orbital IFE dominates, keeping the direction of the total magnetization unchanged.

items.title: Factual recall in linear associative memories: sharp asymptotics and mechanistic insights
items.summary: Large language models excel at factual recall, yet the fundamental limits of storing input--output associations with neural networks remain unclear. We study these limits in a minimal setting: a linear associative memory that maps $p$ input embeddings in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to their $d$-dimensional targets via a linear layer, requiring each mapped input to score its own target above all other outputs. Since all inputs compete for the same outputs, these constraints are strongly correlated, which makes the storage capacity $p_c$ --- the largest number of associations that can be stored --- hard to characterise. We address this in three steps. First, we introduce a decoupled model, in which each input competes with its own independent set of outputs, and provide numerical and analytical evidence that it is equivalent to the original model, both in capacity and in the structure of the learnt solution. Second, using tools from statistical physics, we show that the decoupled model has capacity $p_c \log p_c / d^2 = 1/2$, extend this computation to linear two-layer networks, and go beyond the capacity by predicting the spectrum of the learnt weights and the storage mechanism. The latter explains how the optimal solution outperforms a naïve Hebbian rule: rather than boosting input--output alignments with broad fluctuations, it raises the correct scores just above the extreme-value threshold set by the competing outputs. Third, we prove the decoupled model's capacity thresholds rigorously, including in the non-convex two-layer case; combined with a recent proof for the original model, this shows that both models have the same capacity for full-rank weights. These findings give a sharp characterisation of factual storage in linear networks, and suggest decoupling as a general tool for memorisation and learning problems in which each input must be matched to one of an extensive number of outputs.

items.title: How Rich is the Rich-Club? Super Rich-Club Organization in Complex Networks
items.summary: The rich-club coefficient is used in complex networks to quantify the tendency of progressively higher-degree nodes to be more densely connected than expected by chance. However, it does not capture whether high degree nodes towards the core are actually more interconnected than the original network. Here, we jointly analyze the rich-club coefficient and an enrichment coefficient, which quantifies whether the internal average degree of progressively higher-degree subgraphs is greater than that of the original network, despite the decreasing number of nodes. We apply this framework to real and synthetic networks. Our results reveal three distinct regimes of core organization: rich-club organization without enrichment, enrichment without rich-club organization, and a combination of both, which we call Super Rich-Club organization. In the latter regime, high-degree nodes form cohesive and unusually dense cores that support efficient communication. Our results show that characterizing core organization across structural scales requires considering both relative density and internal connectivity, revealing a stronger form of core organization in real systems with implications for network structure, spectral properties that govern dynamical processes, and communicability.

items.title: Correlation-consistent Gaussian basis sets for copper solids from material-constrained atomic optimization
items.summary: Correlation-consistent Gaussian basis sets are central to systematic molecular quantum chemistry, but their direct use in periodic solids is often limited by severe linear dependence from diffuse atomically optimized primitives. This problem is particularly acute for metallic and metal-containing systems, where reliable complete-basis-set (CBS) extrapolation is needed for correlated-wavefunction benchmarks. We introduce material-constrained atomic optimization (MCAO), a basis-set optimization framework that preserves the atomic and correlation-consistent character of Gaussian basis sets while penalizing large overlap-matrix condition numbers in representative solids. As a proof of concept, we generate Dunning-style MCAO-cc-pVXZ basis sets (X = D, T, Q) for Cu with all-electron, scalar-relativistic all-electron, effective core potential (ECP), and pseudopotential treatments. The resulting basis sets remain numerically stable for Cu solids and surfaces while reproducing molecular Cu dimer energetics and plane-wave reference properties of bulk Cu. CBS-extrapolated random-phase approximation calculations further enable a controlled assessment of pseudopotential, relativistic, and basis-set errors in bulk Cu and CO adsorption on Cu(111), providing scalar-relativistic all-electron Gaussian-basis benchmarks for the CO adsorption puzzle.

items.title: Cost scaling of MPS and TTNS simulations for 2D and 3D systems with area-law entanglement
items.summary: Tensor network states are an indispensable tool for the simulation of strongly correlated quantum many-body systems. In recent years, tree tensor network states (TTNS) have been successfully used for two-dimensional systems and to benchmark quantum simulation approaches for condensed matter, nuclear, and particle physics. In comparison to the more traditional approach based on matrix product states (MPS), the graph distance of physical degrees of freedom can be drastically reduced in TTNS. Surprisingly, it turns out that, for large systems in $D>1$ spatial dimensions, MPS simulations of low-energy states are nevertheless more efficient than TTNS simulations. With a focus on $D=2$ and 3, the scaling of computational costs for different boundary conditions is determined under the assumption that the system obeys an entanglement (log-)area law, implying that bond dimensions scale exponentially in the interface area of the associated subsystems.

items.title: Photonic and Electronic Interaction of TMD-Hybridized ZnO Nanowire Lasers
items.summary: Semiconductor nanowire lasers are promising on-chip coherent light sources for photonic integrated circuits, but integration inevitably places them in contact with other materials, thereby changing their properties upon hybridization. In this study, we examine the photonic and electronic coupling between single ZnO nanowire lasers and TMDs. Using deterministic nanomanipulation, we first hybridized the same nanowire first with a WS$_2$ monolayer and then with a MoS$_2$ monolayer. The respective lasing threshold rises, the emission is strongly quenched at high pump power densities, and the mode envelope blueshifts. Upon hybridization with bilayer, trilayer, and bulk MoS$_2$, lasing is fully suppressed. Finite-Difference Eigenmode simulations show that the TMD absorbs part of the evanescent field. Because this absorption is wavelength dependent, it also removes modes from the low-energy flank of the envelope, which accounts for small difference between the two monolayers, while the blueshift itself follows the increase of the carrier density at threshold. Density functional theory calculations that include the interface dipole predict a type-I alignment at the ideal ZnO(10$\bar{1}$0)/TMD interface, which turns into type~II for a moderately reduced dipole, as expected for hydroxylated facets in air. In both cases, holes are transferred from the nanowire into the TMD and removed from the gain medium. Evanescent absorption and hole transfer thus jointly suppress lasing, and both must be accounted for when integrating nanowire lasers with 2D materials.

items.title: Lifetime of bimerons and antibimerons in two-dimensional magnets
items.summary: Soliton-based computing architectures have recently emerged as a promising avenue to overcome fundamental limitations of conventional information technologies, the von Neumann bottleneck. In this context, magnetic skyrmions have been widely considered for in-situ processing devices due to their mobility and enhanced lifetime in materials with broken inversion symmetry. However, modern applications in non-volatile reservoir or neuromorphic computing raise the additional demand for non-linear inter-soliton interactions. Here, we report that solitons in easy-plane magnets, such as bimerons and antibimerons, show greater versatility and potential for non-linear interactions than skyrmions and antiskyrmions, making them superior candidates for this class of applications. Using first-principles and transition state theory, we predict the coexistence of degenerate bimerons and antibimerons at zero field in a van der Waals heterostructure Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$/Cr$_2$Ge$_2$Te$_6$ -- an experimentally feasible system. We demonstrate that, owing to their distinct structural symmetry, bimerons exhibit fundamentally different behavior from skyrmions and cannot be regarded as their in-plane counterparts, as is often assumed. This distinction leads to unique properties of bimerons and antibimerons, which arise from the unbroken rotational symmetry in easy-plane magnets. These range from anisotropic soliton-soliton interactions to strong entropic effects on their lifetime, driven by the non-local nature of thermal excitations. Our findings reveal a broader richness of solitons in easy-plane magnets and underline their unique potential for spintronic devices.

items.title: Cell-type-specific modularity in E/I networks shapes dynamical regimes and computational capabilities
items.summary: Structural modularity is a ubiquitous feature of brain networks that shapes neural dynamics and information processing. Yet excitatory and inhibitory populations can differ in their modular organization, and it remains unclear how this asymmetry affects network dynamics and computation. Here, using dynamical mean-field theory and simulations of networks performing complex temporal tasks, we show that independently tuning excitatory and inhibitory modularity controls the dynamical regimes of balanced E/I networks. In particular, such tuning can generate a dominant spectral outlier despite overall E/I balance, producing a topology-controlled transition between bulk- and low-rank-dominated regimes, with different dynamical bifurcations leading to chaos and bistability, respectively. In chaotic time-series prediction tasks, computational performance is enhanced near these dynamical boundaries, including both the onset of chaos and the transition to bistability. Favorable configurations exhibit strongly modular excitation and comparatively homogeneous inhibition, similar to what is observed in cortical connectivity.

items.title: A Transient-Network Model of Condensate Aging and Morphology Transition in Phase Separation
items.summary: Biomolecular condensates can undergo striking changes, such as transitioning from a liquid-like to a gel- or a solid-like aggregate due to changes in molecular interactions in response to changes in the biochemical environment. The question of how modified molecular interactions lead to such a transition in the material properties and spatial organization of condensates has not yet been elucidated. To address this question, we represent the biochemical environment as a triphasic mixture comprising a liquid-like protein-rich phase, a network-like protein-rich phase, and solvent. Owing to a change in the biochemical environment, protein molecules can reversibly switch between two conformational states. In a switched conformational state, the cross-linking domains of molecules are exposed which promote transient network formation in phase separated states. We develop a transient-network model and a continuum framework that couples phase separation, molecular switching, and dynamic cross-linking to predict condensate morphology and mechanics. The transient-network model predicts that a non-aging network behaves like a Maxwell fluid. When a network slowly ages via stabilization of cross-links, it shows Maxwell-like behavior and waiting time-dependent relaxation. However, a strongly aged network shows elastic recoil like characteristic of a Kelvin-Voigt solid. Our coupled continuum model demonstrates that the interplay of molecular switching and dynamic cross-linking in network formation shapes the spatial organization of condensate phases. In summary, this work demonstrates a mechanistic route explaining how conformational switching and molecular cross-linking regulate material properties and morphology of condensates.

items.title: Anisotropic Nanoscale Coherent Polariton Transport in CrSBr
authors: Paritosh Malik, Dogyun Ko, Vita Solovyeva, Chirag C. Palekar, Imad Limame, Sven Rodt, Kseniia Mosina, Zdeněk Sofer, Alexander Steinhoff, Martin Esmann, Stephan Reitzenstein, Bo Han, Christopher Gies, and Christian Schneider
items.summary: Abstract In a combined experimental and theoretical study, we demonstrate anisotropic polariton transport on the nanoscale in the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr. While effective cavity-polariton formation emerges via the self-hybridization of ultrahigh oscillator strength excitons with a thin slab photonic mode, the absence of external mirrors facilitates spectroscopic investigation of these polaritons via cathodoluminescence (CL) on length scales inaccessible to optical excitation. This direct access allows us to precisely chart the polariton landscape with nanometric resolution, and probe polariton interference phenomena. Our finding highlights that coherent polariton transport follows the C 2v symmetry of CrSBr, highly directional transport along the a -axis, while no coherent features are found along the b -axis. By extending CL spectroscopy to strongly anisotropic cavity polaritons, our work establishes this technique as a powerful tool to probe highly directional expansion and relaxation phenomena on the nanoscale, paving the way for investigating complex polaritonic landscapes in asymmetric systems.

items.title: Divalent Cations Induce Rigid and Compact Structures in Underwound DNA
authors: Aleksander Klimczyk, Dorothy Aboagye-Mensah, and Graeme A. King
items.summary: Abstract Negative supercoiling (underwinding) of DNA plays a vital role in regulating genome organization and gene expression. These processes often depend on the DNA structure, yet the influence of ionic strength on supercoiled DNA structure is still not well understood. Here, we develop an approach to extract detailed insight into the mechanical properties of underwound DNA from force–distance measurements. Using this approach, we demonstrate that low concentrations (2 mM) of divalent cations are sufficient to induce substantial increases in DNA persistence length at high superhelical densities. This is consistent with the formation of Z-DNA, a rigid, left-handed conformation, and suggests that Z-DNA-like structures can be more readily formed than is often assumed. We also show that divalent cations can induce extensive sawtooth-like behavior in force–extension curves of underwound DNA, revealing unexpectedly strong stabilization of secondary structures. Together, these findings demonstrate how divalent salt can sensitively modulate the stability of different underwound structures.

items.title: Majorana-like Josephson branch structure in one-dimensional transport of cold atoms
items.summary: We study phase-controlled transport through a one-dimensional channel of attractively interacting fermions connecting two three-dimensional BCS reservoirs. The competition between channel phase stiffness and pair tunnelling at the two contacts results in the emergence of two $4π$-periodic families of stationary states, characterised by symmetric or asymmetric phase drops at the boundaries. Advancing the reservoir phase difference by $2π$ exchanges these families so that the equilibrium energy remains $2π$ periodic, while the $4π$ periodicity might be attained in a diabatic regime. This structure admits a formal description in terms of two boundary Majorana operators, combining into a nonlocal fermion mode. Renormalization-group analysis shows that quantum fluctuations and phase slips are suppressed in the zero-temperature thermodynamic limit, preserving the branch crossings. The predicted branch exchange, metastable currents, and sweep-rate-dependent switching provide experimentally testable signatures of Majorana-like Josephson branch physics in a gapless interacting channel.

items.title: Electronic liquid crystals and superconductivity from doping a moiré Mott insulator
items.summary: Electronic liquid crystals, such as stripe phases and nematics, are self-organized states of matter with spontaneously broken rotational symmetry. They are expected to emerge in a doped Mott insulator as a compromise between short- and long-range Coulomb interactions, and are believed to be intimately connected to the emergence of high temperature superconductivity either as a competing order or an intertwined order. Moiré semiconductors provide a controllable platform to explore the relationship between stripe phases and superconductivity near a Mott insulator. Here we report the generic appearance of stripe phases in a doped moiré Mott insulator and the observation of a stripe to-superconductor quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer WSe2. The stripe phases were revealed by electrical transport studies as a thermodynamic phase transition from a high temperature isotropic phase to a low-temperature anisotropic phase accompanied by a Fermi surface reconstruction. Near the stripe-to-superconductor transition, we also observed an additional thermodynamic phase transition from metallic stripes to pinned insulating stripes. The stripe-to-superconductor transition further exhibits an intriguing self-similarity that highlights the intimate relationship between the two orders. Our results pave the path for studying intertwined orders in moiré materials.

items.title: Millikelvin magnetometry up to 30~T using a multi-cross micro-Hall sensor
items.summary: We report a multi-cross micro-Hall sensor fabricated from an MBE-grown GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure for high-sensitivity magnetometry. The device enables dc magnetization measurements at temperatures down to $\sim$15~mK and in dc magnetic fields up to 30 T. Bulk samples with dimensions ranging from 100~$μ$m to 1~mm can be measured with a resolution better than 1$~μ$T with a 1~$μ$A excitation at 13.77 Hz. Test-of-performance measurements were carried out by probing the field-dependent magnetization plateaus of the triangular-lattice quantum magnet K$_{2}$Co$_{2}$(SeO$_{3}$)$_{3}$ at 20~mK, the antiferromagnetic transition of K${_3}$GdTe${_2}$O${_9}$ near 220 mK via temperature-dependent magnetization, and the quantum oscillations in a ruthenium single crystal. A simple and reliable sample-mounting setup that ensures reproducible magnetic measurements is provided.

items.title: First-principles study of the formation of Group-IV--vacancy color centers in diamond
items.summary: $XV$ ($X$ is Si, Ge, Sn, or Pb, and $V$ is the carbon vacancy) color centers are promising platforms for quantum computing and quantum information science due to their favorable optical and spin properties. They are commonly fabricated by ion implantation, which inevitably introduces vacancies and carbon self-interstitials (C$_i$) into the lattice. However, the microscopic formation mechanism remains unclear, limiting the yield and stability of $XV$ centers. Here, first-principles calculations are conducted to systematically investigate the roles of $V$ and C$_i$ in $XV$ formation. We find that $XV$ formation is energetically favorable, with large binding energies and low diffusion barriers. Nevertheless, $XV$ readily captures C$_i$ to form substitutional defect $X_s$, or captures an additional $V$ to form the complex $XV_2$. Charge transition levels show that oppositely charged reactants never meet in these reactions, and that Coulomb repulsion blocks them only when both reactants carry charges of the same sign, which for the capture of C$_i$ requires strongly n- or p-type conditions. These competing defect reactions destabilize the split-vacancy configuration and could account for the low formation yield of $XV$ centers, so that they appear at concentrations well below those expected from the implanted dose. Our results elucidate the microscopic origin of this intrinsic instability and suggest that Fermi-level control may suppress defect conversions and stabilize the split-vacancy configuration.

items.title: Anomalous thermal transport in isotope-enriched germanium carbide
items.summary: Advances in modern electronics demand the dissipation of heat fluxes approaching 1000 W cm$^{-2}$, which drives an urgent need for materials with thermal conductivity ($κ$) exceeding 1000 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. Here, by solving the Boltzmann transport equation considering both three- and four-phonon interactions, we observe that isotopically pure cubic germanium carbide (GeC) exhibits a remarkable $κ$ of 1018 W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ at room temperature, which is further corroborated by state-of-the-art machine-learning molecular dynamics simulations. Two unique mechanisms underlie this anomalously high $κ$: a remarkably strong isotopic enhancement effect (289%) and a surprisingly modest suppression due to four-phonon scattering (22%)-despite the presence of a wide acoustic-optical phonon gap. Moreover, we find that GeC defies the conventional Leibfried-Schlomann formula and exhibits a non-monotonic variation of $κ$ with external hydrostatic pressure at elevated temperatures. Our findings establish isotope-enriched GeC as a material of ultrahigh $κ$ and an ideal platform for exploring exotic phonon physics.

items.title: Ta-based S-I-S junctions for integrated superconducting electronics
items.summary: In this work, we have presented S-I-S Josephson junctions with $\rmα$-Ta electrodes and a ${\rm TaO}_x$ barrier. We grew base and top $α$-Ta electrodes using seed layer engineering, showing both Nb and ${\rm TaN}_x$ are viable seed layer choices, and particularly emphasize that at room temperature a re-seed layer is required to nucleate $\rmα$-Ta for the top electrode. However, we note that the choice of seed layer can have subtle implications on the electrical tunneling behavior of the junctions. We used room-temperature probing of variable junction areas, combined with Ambegaokar-Baratoff physics, to characterize the wafer scale critical current densities. For 0.4 $μ$m$^2$ junctions, we found junction spreads as low as 2.0% across the 20 x 20 mm chip relevant for device performance. The entire process was carried out using standard industry foundry processing using 150 mm wafer tooling, which is an important step towards proving that Ta-based junctions can be implemented at scale. We have successfully fabricated and tested junctions with $\rmα$-Ta electrodes and a ${\rm TaO}_x$ insulating tunnel barrier, demonstrating that this is a material platform which merits further investigation and studies for potential application in classical and quantum superconducting technologies.

items.title: Explicit pore pre-conditioning and inverse design of amorphous nanoporous carbon
items.summary: Porous carbons store energy, capture gases and purify water, and their performance depends strongly on the geometry of their pores. Atomistic models mostly simulate their synthesis by molecular dynamics, with results that depend on the interatomic potential, and return the pore network as an output rather than as a specification. Here we show that the pore network can be an input: pores drawn from a target size distribution fill a prescribed volume fraction, carbon is grown around them by stochastic ring placement, and a particle swarm recovers the construction parameters from a structural fingerprint. The search reproduces the density, surface area and pore volume of a carbon produced by quenched molecular dynamics within about 5 %, together with its pore size distribution. As a stress test, it also recovers a bimodal distribution, and the search history reveals which parameters the targets constrain and flags a failed search. A short anneal completes the network, recovering the coordination of the reference while the pore size distribution keeps its shape. Molecular dynamics still supplies the local chemistry, but the pore geometry becomes a design variable for a given application.

items.title: Streptavidin–Biotin Binding Is Intrinsically Noncooperative, but Experimental Artifacts Can Induce Apparent Positive Cooperativity
authors: Malavika Kayyil Veedu, Eléonore Martenne Duplan, Saurabh Rai, Prithu Roy, and Jérôme Wenger
items.summary: Abstract The biotin–streptavidin interaction is a key component of nanobiotechnology, yet the nature of its cooperativity remains a debated question. Here, we introduce a label-free spectroscopy approach based on confocal UV autofluorescence microscopy to probe the binding cooperativity of this high-affinity system. By leveraging the intrinsic autofluorescence of tryptophan residues, we avoid artifacts associated with extrinsic fluorescent labels, enabling precise measurements of fully biotin-saturated streptavidin across a wide range of molar ratios. Our experimental results, supported by Monte Carlo simulations, provide conclusive evidence for the absence of cooperativity. However, we show that false signs of apparent positive cooperativity can emerge from local concentration inhomogeneities occurring when rapid reaction kinetics outpace mixing. By establishing the noncooperative nature of biotin–streptavidin binding and identifying the key conditions to avoid cooperativity artifacts, these insights resolve a longstanding debate and offer critical implications for streptavidin-based biotechnological applications.

items.title: Cryogenic suppression of correlated loss in Rydberg atom arrays
items.summary: Blackbody radiation (BBR) poses a central challenge for quantum science with Rydberg atoms. By driving transitions to nearby opposite-parity states, BBR shortens Rydberg lifetimes and has long been suspected to trigger "avalanche" events known to cause correlated atom loss. Here, we suppress avalanche decay and establish BBR as its dominant trigger using a Rydberg atom array that operates either cryogenically or at room temperature. A $45~\text{K}$ radiation shield reduces ambient BBR, extending Rydberg $nS$ lifetimes for $n$ ranging from 50 to 75. BBR-induced decay rates are suppressed by 30%-50%, corresponding to an effective blackbody temperature $T_{\rm eff}\approx190~\text{K}$. This enables controlled comparisons of Rydberg-dressed atom arrays operating in different BBR environments. Arrays of up to 70 atoms demonstrate cryogenically suppressed avalanche rates, tracking the suppression in BBR-induced decay, for both $n=50$ and $n=60$ dressing. A parameter-free rate model agrees with the measured avalanche rates after accounting for frequency-dependent cryogenic shielding, photoionization-triggered avalanches, laser phase noise, BBR decay channels, and Rydberg interaction effects. We demonstrate a quantitative description of avalanche decay and show that improved BBR shielding should further suppress correlated loss to the $T_\text{eff}=45~\text{K}$ achievable in the current apparatus. Our results establish a route to mitigating correlated errors that otherwise impede fault-tolerant operation in neutral-atom quantum processors.

items.title: Free electrons unveil nanolaser physics at the sub-picosecond and nanometer scale
items.summary: Semiconducting nanowire lasers (NWLs) constitute nanoscale modular and tunable light sources, essential components for integrated optoelectronics. However, advancing NWL operation requires characterization of their near-field and dynamics at the nanometer scale, which is hampered by the diffraction limit of light. Here, we show a non-perturbative measurement of the absolute number of photons in a GaN/InGaN nanowire nanolaser cavity above the lasing threshold with sub-picosecond resolution and maps of the lasing mode spatial profile at the nanoscale. For this we use photon-induced near-field electron microscopy while simultaneously measuring the photons far-field, unraveling the key nanoscale and time-resolved characteristics of a NWL in operation. With this technique, we observed lasing with a pump-power-dependent time offset of 0.5-1 ps that reflects carrier thermalization and spontaneous emission, and a pulse duration of 500 to 700 fs. From the spatial maps of the lasing mode, we observe TM-polarized azimuthal whispering gallery modes along the nanowire circumference, as well as two distinct Fabry-Perot modes along the nanowire length. These spatial maps allow us to understand which of the multiple complex cavity modes available in the nanowire are responsible for lasing paving the way for their practical application into devices.

items.title: IceCube data for astrophysical neutrinos exhibit q-statistical behavior
items.summary: Relevant IceCube recent data for astrophysical neutrinos are analyzed. Similarly to cosmic rays and proton-proton LHC collisions, the corresponding spectra are satisfactorily described, for the entire interval of measured energies, through $q$-Gaussians. This fact reinforces the already available evidence that nonadditive entropies (either of the $S_q$ class or of the $S_δ$ one, or even alternative ones) appear to play a crucial role in systems such as black holes and related cosmological phenomena (e.g., dark energy). The IceCube data yield high values for the momenta-distribution nonadditive index ($q \simeq 1.6$, hence $q_{energy} \simeq 1.3$), to be compared with the cosmic rays values ($q_{energy} \simeq 1.2$) and the LHC values ($q_{energy} \simeq 1.1$). This fact neatly indicates very-long-ranged space-time correlations. The detailed associated physical mechanisms remain, at the present stage, as an instigating open issue.

items.title: Finite-width shift of the edge of chaos in deep neural networks
items.summary: Deep neural networks train best when they are initialised at the edge of chaos, the critical line in the plane of weight and bias variances on which the distance between two inputs neither grows nor shrinks with depth. The line is known for infinitely wide networks; at finite width it moves, and how it moves has been disputed. We treat the logarithm of the distance between two inputs through a network of width $N$ as a random walk and compute its drift and variance to order $1/N$. The edge of chaos moves to a larger weight variance, by $Δσ_w^2=-a_1/(N\,\partial_{σ_w^2}\lnχ_1)$, about $8/N$ for $\tanh$ networks at a bias variance of $0.05$, confirmed by simulations of the exact finite-width recursion.
